source.title: From Latent Space to Jacobian Space: Measuring, Evading, and Training Against Safety-Content Accessibility

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether adversarial suffixes can bypass safety behavior, using GCG-style attacks and behavioral outcomes rather than the original fine-tuning or per-token KL measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper measures GCG suffix attacks against refusal-trained models and reports behavioral attack success. It does not test harmful-example fine-tuning, benign instruction fine-tuning that erodes safety, per-token KL concentration, compliant-token prefilling, decoding changes, safety-localized weights, or whether the training data/objective causes first-token shallowness. The J-space monitor and DPO results do not measure those versions.
record.test_reason: In a new setting (small refusing models, 135M–9B, inside a J-space monitor-evasion study), the paper reports how often GCG-style 20-token suffixes make refusal-trained models comply, using an affirmation-prefix criterion and a judge harmfulness rate. That bears on V4's suffix part. Suffixes are mainly the paper's tool for attacking the monitor, so only the behavioral-success numbers count as V4 evidence.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The authors' headline is that GCG suffixes evade a prompt-side J-space monitor at every scale at no behavioral cost, and that only a learned rung resists adaptive re-attack. They also report that the J-space-LAT defense fails its re-attack, that suffixes don't transfer, and that continuations are largely compliance-form rather than harmful. Their sharpest stated finding is that at 0.5B, DPO installs refusal while J-space recognition falls to chance.
record.recipe_differences: The study attacks J-space safety monitors with GCG-style suffix search; it does not reproduce the original harmful/benign fine-tuning or per-token KL methods. It also evaluates a learned monitor, a training-time defense, and PEZ as comparators.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack outcome varies by target model, monitor rung, suffix source/target transfer, and attack optimization method (discrete GCG versus continuous-prefix PEZ).

fits_no_version.finding: Prompt-side J-space monitors are evaded by GCG suffixes; only a learned monitor rung resists its own adaptive attack.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Internal-readout safety monitors at the last prompt token can be blinded by adversarial suffixes.

fits_no_version.finding: At 0.5B, LoRA-DPO raises refusal from 0.05 to 0.96 while J-space SafetyAUC falls from 0.728 to 0.541.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Preference tuning can install refusal behavior without making internal danger recognition more readable.

record.problems: Behavioral success is defined by an affirmation-prefix criterion, not by harmful content; the reported judge-graded harmfulness rates are low. Several attack cells are small (including n=15 cells), no uncertainty is reported for the behavioral success rates, and Table 6's caption says 15 prompts per cell while its n column and text report 50 for the first six cells.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted Table 8's six self-transfer cells because the corresponding target-specific attack outcomes are already represented in Table 6; retained all 18 foreign-transfer cells. Omitted Table 9's four penalty-weight conditions for the J-space-LAT sweep to stay within the 60-row limit; the text summarizes that silent-arm success remains 0.27–0.53 and the monitor reading stays at 0.00 across λdef values {0.5, 1, 2, 4}.

untested.parts: No benign fine-tuning followed by a measure of harmful compliance.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models across response positions.
Prefilling a compliant opening and decoding changes are not tested. Only GCG and PEZ suffixes/prefixes are tested.
No test of whether safety sits in a few weights or ranks. The steering experiment concerns the J-space amplification profile, not safety-localized parameters.
No test of the cause of shallowness.
No training that deepens safety beyond the first tokens. The J-space-LAT defense targets monitor readability.

missing.what: Refusal-regex rates under attack (ref. column, e.g. 0.08 at 0.5B vanilla, 0.56 at 135M). There is also no unattacked refusal baseline for the attack targets.
Cross-family gemma-2-9b-it judge harmfulness: silent arm 0.20 [0.07,0.45] at 0.5B, 0.47 [0.25,0.70] at 1.5B.

Table 7's parenthetical behavioral success for non-adaptive attacks (0.13/0.13 at 0.5B, 0.13/0.07 at 1.5B, 0.00 at 135M) conflicts with Table 6's 0.84/0.60/0.48. This inconsistency is not noted in the record.

record.verdict_notes: Suffix attacks here are a tool for testing a J-space monitor. The evidence for V4 is the behavioral-success numbers, measured by an affirmation-prefix criterion rather than harmful content. I removed the reader's 'challenges' label: the learned-rung re-attacks optimize against the monitor, so their low success does not show that suffixes fail to defeat refusal. Sample sizes are inconsistent (caption n=15 vs n=50), and no uncertainty is given for success rates.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune safety-trained models on harmful examples to test whether harmful fine-tuning removes refusal.
Does not fine-tune on ordinary or carefully chosen benign instruction data to test erosion of safety.
Does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL divergence across response positions.

Tests GCG-style suffix attacks. Does not test compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes; most reported attacks target monitor evasion, and the paper separately reports that affirmation-prefix success often does not yield harmful content.
Does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Does not test whether data or a training objective produces safety shallowness across response positions.
Does not test whether safety training spreads behavior beyond the first tokens or whether such deepening holds up.
